summary.text:
A different shape from anything else in the library. City Fund has no external borrowing at all — the authorised limit for borrowing is £0 and actual debt is £0, with only £35.0m of IFRS 16 lease liabilities. The £450m of variable rate market debt sits in City's Estate and has not moved since 2019/20. Treasury balances are £920.6m.

The interesting mechanic is the split strategy. Since April 2022 City Fund has run the full range of investments including short-dated bond funds, while every other fund is restricted to specified investments. The result is two yields for the same year: 4.60% for City Fund against 3.87% for the rest, a 73 basis point spread that is a direct read on what the extra latitude bought. The bond funds themselves returned -0.03% on capital, having distributed £7.6m of interest.

One fact here is worth carrying to every HRA council we write to: paragraph 14 records that the PWLB HRA rate, 40 basis points over gilts, has been extended to March 2027. Stoke's report, written in February, still had it ending March 2026. One officer address is published, and their Audit and Risk Management Committee takes this report on 14 September.

officer.subject: The HRA rate extension, and your 73 basis point spread
officer.body:
Hi Sarah,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts ahead of Audit and Risk Management on 14 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

Yours is the only report in this month's reading where the answer to "what's the borrowing position" is nil. City Fund's authorised limit for borrowing is £0, actual external debt is £0, and the only long-term liability is £35.0m of IFRS 16 leases. That's an unusual place to be standing with £920.6m of treasury balances.

Two things in the report caught our attention, and one of them we're going to reuse.

The reusable one is paragraph 14. You record that the PWLB HRA rate, 40 basis points over gilts, has been extended to March 2027. Every other council we've read this month that mentions it — including one writing in February — still had it ending March 2026. That's a genuinely useful fact for any authority with an HRA borrowing decision in front of it, and yours is the paper that carries it.

The other is the bifurcated strategy. Splitting the Annual Investment Strategy in 2022, so City Fund takes the full range including short-dated bond funds while every other fund is restricted to specified investments, has produced two yields for the same year: 4.60% against 3.87%. A 73 basis point spread is about as clean a read as you'll get on what the extra latitude actually bought, and it's the sort of number most councils can't isolate because they've only got one strategy. Worth noting that the bond funds themselves returned -0.03% on capital while distributing £7.6m of interest — the yield came from income, not price.

On the borrowing side, paragraph 15 says the City Fund CFR is expected to increase and at least part of the need will be met internally. When that stops being the cheaper option is the question, and the answer moves with the curve: ten-year certainty money is 5.83% today against 5.72% at the end of March, and fifty-year 6.27% against 6.08%. Bank Rate is 3.75% with the one-year OIS around 4.11%, so your July view that markets are pricing a hike into December 2026 or early 2027 is holding.

The rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard takes ten seconds, both fixings, whole curve, and the monthly sector breakdown at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity shows what the market is drawing: July was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers, average 5.02%. If City's Estate ever needs its £450m priced against the DMO's repayment curve, that's at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On training, three fit the Corporation: Cost of carry and internal borrowing, for the position paragraph 13 describes; PWLB rates and the certainty discount; and our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes, and directly relevant to a rising CFR met internally. For members, Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) is written for exactly the committee this goes to. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
